title: Wispr Flow raises $280M Series B at $2B, ships its own Canto speech model
subtitle: Menlo Ventures leads a bottom-up dictation company past 125,000 businesses, and Wispr replaces its third-party speech stack with an in-house model that cuts noisy-room error rates from 30 percent to under 10.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Wispr closed a $280 million Series B on August 17 at a $2 billion valuation, led by Menlo Ventures, bringing total funding to $361 million less than 10 months after its previous round. Alongside the raise the company launched Canto, its first proprietary speech-to-text model. In noisy real-world conditions Wispr says Canto cuts word error rates from more than 30 percent to between 5 and 10, replacing the third-party speech stack that Wispr Flow had used since launch. Existing backers Notable Capital, NEA, Neo Ventures, 8VC and MVP Ventures doubled down; Acrew, Forerunner, Goodwater, Peak XV, Together Fund and PLUS Capital joined as new investors.

What makes this raise interesting is the distribution model behind it. Wispr Flow — the desktop and mobile app that turns speech into formatted text across any application — reached 125,000 businesses and most of the Fortune 500 largely through employees adopting it on their own, not through top-down enterprise sales. That kind of individual-contributor pull is rare for a productivity tool priced at seat scale, and the Canto launch is the company's answer to the main complaint that pull was starting to generate: accuracy drift in real environments. Moving the model in-house lets Wispr tune the acoustic model to its own usage data instead of waiting on a general-purpose provider.

Voice input has been the promised-then-postponed interface for at least a decade, and most of the wins so far have come inside specific verticals — medical dictation, call centers, in-car. What is different about this cycle is that the language model on the other side of the microphone is finally good enough to do the cleanup — the ums, the reformatting, the tone shift — that made raw transcription feel unusable in general software. Menlo's bet, in the round's framing, is that the text box is on its way out as the default input for knowledge work.

A takeaway for learners: interfaces change when three things line up — the input capture gets accurate enough, the cleanup layer gets smart enough, and someone builds a distribution model that does not depend on a purchase order. Voice has waited on the third one for a long time. Watch which productivity tools you or your team adopt without asking permission over the next twelve months. That signal is a better indicator of what stays than any analyst chart.
